title: More than just a game
text: When most people think of Minecraft, they imagine someone building a house, digging for diamonds or running away from a creeper. With more than three hundred million copies sold, it is the best-selling video game of all time, and for millions of players that is exactly what it is: a fun way to spend an afternoon. Yet over the years, a growing number of people have discovered that this world of blocks can be used for things its creators probably never imagined.

Take redstone, for example. In the game, redstone is a red dust that carries power, a little like electricity. At first, players used it to open doors or switch on lamps. Then some of them realised that, by combining it in clever ways, they could build the same logic gates that are found inside real computers. Before long, enthusiasts were constructing working calculators, and later entire computers, block by block. In 2022, one player even built a machine inside Minecraft that could run a simple version of Minecraft itself.

Such projects can take months of patient work, and they are not just impressive tricks. Many of the people who build them say they learnt more about how computers work from redstone than from any textbook. Because every wire and switch is visible, the game turns abstract ideas into something you can walk around and touch, at least on a screen.

Teachers soon noticed this potential. In 2016, an Education Edition of the game was launched, designed specifically for schools. Today it is used in classrooms all over the world to teach subjects as different as chemistry, history and programming. Pupils might recreate an ancient city, experiment with elements in a virtual laboratory or write simple code that makes a robot build a bridge. Supporters argue that students who would normally lose interest become fully involved, simply because the lesson takes place in a world they already love.

Perhaps the most surprising use of Minecraft, however, has nothing to do with science. In 2020, the organisation Reporters Without Borders opened the Uncensored Library, an enormous digital building inside the game. Its shelves contain articles by journalists whose work has been banned in their own countries. The idea was clever: in places where news websites are blocked, Minecraft is often still available, so young people can find the articles by visiting the library in the game.

Not everyone is convinced, of course. Some parents and teachers worry that using games in education makes it even harder for children to concentrate on traditional lessons, and that time spent in front of a screen should be limited, not increased. Others point out that a game cannot replace a good teacher, however popular it is.

Even so, it is difficult to deny that Minecraft has become something unusual: a tool as much as a toy. The blocks are the same for everyone, but what people build with them depends entirely on their imagination. And if a group of players can build a computer, a classroom and a library out of nothing but virtual cubes, it is hard to say where the limits really are.

grammar.rule: Four parts like the Use of English paper of the Cambridge B2 First exam. Parts 2, 3 and 4: write your answers and press Check.

parts.title: Part 1 · Multiple-choice cloze
parts.help: Read the text and choose the word or phrase that best fits each gap.
parts.text: When Minecraft first {{0}} out, few people expected it to become a worldwide phenomenon. Instead of following instructions, they could {{3}} up their own minds about what to build. This sense of freedom is still the main {{4}} why so many people play it today. In {{5}}, many of the most famous creations were made by players who simply wanted to see what was possible.

parts.title: Part 2 · Open cloze
parts.help: Write one word in each gap.
parts.text: Building a computer in Minecraft is {{6}} an easy task. First, you need to understand the basic logic {{7}} all computers use. parts.help: Use the word in capitals at the end of each gap to form a word that fits.
